definition: A model describing matter as being made up of tiny particles that are constantly moving. Explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
clues: This is a model used in physics and chemistry
It describes matter as tiny moving particles
It explains differences between states of matter
A model of matter describing all substances as tiny particles in constant motion — explains properties of solids, liquids and gases

definition: A state of matter where particles are closely packed in a regular lattice, vibrating in fixed positions. Has a definite shape and volume.
clues: This is a state of matter
The particles are closely packed and vibrate in fixed positions
It has a definite shape and volume
Particles packed in a regular lattice, vibrating in fixed positions — cannot flow or be compressed; has a fixed shape and volume

definition: A state of matter where particles are close together but can move around each other. Has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
clues: This is a state of matter
Particles are close together but can move past each other
It takes the shape of its container
Particles touching but free to move — has a fixed volume but flows to fill the shape of its container; cannot be significantly compressed

definition: A state of matter where particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds. Has no fixed shape or volume; fills its container.
clues: This is a state of matter
Particles are far apart and move randomly
It fills the container it is in
Widely spaced particles moving randomly at high speed — can be compressed, flows easily and fills any container it is placed in

definition: Mass per unit volume of a material. ρ = m/V. Measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³. Solids are usually denser than liquids, which are denser than gases.
clues: This is a property of materials
It compares mass to volume
It is measured in kg/m³
Mass per unit volume — ρ = m/V; solids are usually most dense, then liquids, then gases

definition: The change of state from solid to liquid. Occurs at the melting point when particles gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions.
clues: This is a change of state
It is the transition from solid to liquid
Energy is absorbed during this process
Solid → liquid — particles gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions; occurs at the melting point

definition: The change of state from liquid to gas, occurring throughout the liquid at a specific temperature (the boiling point). Requires energy input.
clues: This is a change of state
It is the transition from liquid to gas
It happens throughout a liquid at a fixed temperature
Liquid → gas occurring throughout the liquid at the boiling point — requires energy input to overcome intermolecular forces

definition: The change of state from gas to liquid. Occurs when gas particles lose energy and slow down enough to form attractions with other particles.
clues: This is a change of state
It is the transition from gas to liquid
Energy is released during this process
Gas → liquid — particles lose energy and slow down, forming attractive forces; energy is released to the surroundings

definition: The change of state from liquid to solid. Occurs when particles lose enough energy to settle into fixed positions.
clues: This is a change of state
It is the transition from liquid to solid
Energy is released during this process
Liquid → solid — particles lose energy and slow down until they lock into fixed lattice positions; energy is released

definition: The change of state directly from solid to gas, without passing through the liquid state. Example: dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimes at room temperature.
clues: This is an unusual change of state
It goes directly from solid to gas
Dry ice is an example
A solid turning directly into a gas — no liquid stage; dry ice (CO₂) and iodine crystals sublime under certain conditions

definition: The energy needed to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature. Two types: latent heat of fusion (melting/freezing) and latent heat of vaporisation (boiling/condensing).
clues: This is a type of energy involved in changes of state
The temperature does not change while this energy is transferred
It comes in two types: fusion and vaporisation
Energy transferred during a change of state that does not raise temperature — it breaks or forms forces between particles

definition: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. L = Q/m. Unit: J/kg.
clues: This is a property of substances related to changes of state
It is measured in J/kg
It does not involve a temperature change
The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance — L = Q/m; no temperature change occurs during the process

definition: The energy needed to melt (or freeze) 1 kg of a substance at its melting point.
clues: This is a specific type of latent heat
It applies to melting and freezing
It measures energy per kilogram
The energy required to melt 1 kg of a substance at its melting point — the same energy is released when 1 kg freezes

definition: The energy needed to boil (or condense) 1 kg of a substance at its boiling point.
clues: This is a specific type of latent heat
It applies to boiling and condensing
It is typically much larger than the latent heat of fusion
The energy required to vaporise 1 kg of liquid at its boiling point — much larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance

definition: The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a substance. Increasing temperature increases internal energy.
clues: This is a concept in physics
It is the total energy of all particles in a substance
It increases when a substance is heated
The sum of kinetic and potential energy of all particles — temperature measures average kinetic energy; adding heat increases internal energy

definition: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Measured in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K).
clues: This is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles
It is measured in °C or K
Higher values mean particles move faster on average
A measure of the mean kinetic energy of particles — not the same as internal energy, which also depends on the number of particles

definition: The force exerted per unit area by gas molecules colliding with the walls of their container. Increases with temperature or decreased volume.
clues: This is a property of gases
It is caused by particles colliding with the walls of a container
It increases when temperature rises
The force per unit area exerted by gas molecules hitting container walls — increases when temperature rises or volume decreases

definition: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
clues: This is a law relating pressure and volume of a gas
It applies at constant temperature
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional
At constant temperature, doubling the pressure halves the volume — P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; more compression means more collisions per unit area

definition: For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature. P/T = constant.
clues: This is a law relating pressure and temperature of a gas
It applies at constant volume
Pressure and absolute temperature are directly proportional
At constant volume, increasing temperature increases pressure — P/T = constant; higher temperature means faster particles and harder collisions

definition: The lowest possible temperature (0 K = −273°C) at which particles have minimum internal energy and exert no pressure.
clues: This is the lowest possible temperature
It is equal to −273°C or 0 kelvin
At this temperature, particles have minimum energy
The temperature at which gas pressure would reach zero — 0 K or −273°C; particles have the minimum possible energy

definition: An absolute temperature scale starting at absolute zero (0 K). 0 K = −273°C. To convert: K = °C + 273.
clues: This is a temperature scale used in physics
It starts at absolute zero
To convert from Celsius, add 273
The absolute temperature scale — 0 K = −273°C; used in gas law calculations where temperature must not be negative

definition: The random, unpredictable movement of small particles (e.g. pollen or smoke) suspended in a fluid, caused by bombardment from moving molecules.
clues: This is a type of motion observed in small particles
It provides evidence for the particle model
It is caused by collisions from invisible molecules
Random jiggling of tiny particles in a fluid — caused by unequal bombardment from fast-moving molecules; evidence for the particle model

definition: The change of state from liquid to gas that occurs at the surface of a liquid below its boiling point. Faster-moving particles escape from the surface.
clues: This is a change of state that occurs at the surface of a liquid
It can happen below the boiling point
It cools the remaining liquid
Liquid → gas from the surface only, at any temperature — the fastest particles escape, leaving cooler ones behind and reducing the temperature
